title: History made! Obama taps Lori Robinson as first woman ever to lead a U.S. combatant command
text: A glass ceiling is about to shatter. President Barack Obama will name the first woman ever to head a U.S. combatant command, choosing Air Force General Lori Robinson to take over the military's powerful Northern Command, Defense Secretary Ash Carter revealed on Friday. The job, which still needs Senate confirmation, is one of the most senior in the entire U.S. military. It would make Robinson - who currently leads U.S. air forces in the Pacific - the top general overseeing activities in North America. Who could miss the significance? “General Robinson, it just so happens, would also be the first ever female combatant commander,” Carter said, letting slip Obama's plans to nominate her. “That shows yet another thing - which is that we have, coming along now, a lot of female officers who are exceptionally strong. And Lori certainly fits into that category,” Carter said at an event hosted by Politico. And that was not the only big move! Carter also announced that Army General Vincent Brooks, the commanding general of U.S. Army Pacific, would be nominated as the next commander of U.S. Forces in South Korea.

title: D.C. guidance sets possible fines for misuse of transgender employees' names and pronouns
text: Following the leftist agenda is no longer optional in the District of Columbia; those who do not follow the rules may be subject to fines. According to the guide, the District uses the probable cause standard in determining whether the conduct described constitutes harassment or a hostile work environment. Stephanie Franklin, the OHR's interim director of policy and communications, confirmed in an email that any workplace environment in D.C., private businesses included, in which supervisors or co-workers deliberately misuse a person's preferred name or pronoun may be considered unlawful harassment and/or a hostile work environment under D.C. law. The best practices guide features a chart on gender and gender-neutral pronouns, including the gender-neutral pronoun ze. The chart gives example phrases using that pronoun, such as "Ze smiled", "I met zir", "Zir bike" and "Ze is zirself". The guide states that, regardless of an employee's legal name and gender, employers should use the employee's desired name and pronouns when communicating with them and when referring to them in conversations with third parties. It also says that the employer must ensure employees respect and use a transgender employee's preferred names and pronouns, because repeated failure to do so can be considered harassment and can cause severe distress to a transgender employee. The guide further states that employees should be allowed to use the bathroom in which they are most comfortable, and that transgender employees should at all times be able to use the restroom and other gender-segregated facilities, such as locker rooms, that they are most comfortable with. In the 2015 fiscal year, 307 discrimination complaints, including race, gender and disability complaints, ended in settlements through mediation. According to the annual report, more than $3.69 million was awarded in settlements during successful mediations in 2015, a 74 percent increase over the 2014 fiscal year.

title: Shrinking paychecks: How inflation quietly stole overtime pay from American workers
text: President Obama is going it alone on labor policy yet again, and this time the target is overtime. The Labor Department is expected in the coming weeks to unveil a rule that would make millions more Americans eligible for overtime. Right now, only workers earning below $455 a week, or $23,660 a year, are guaranteed time-and-a-half pay for working more than 40 hours a week. Think about that. The law may push that line as high as $52,000, Politico reports. The rule would also rewrite the regulations on which employees above that threshold qualify; at the moment, employers can exempt some of them if those workers could be considered "white collar." It would be the latest in a string of workplace policies that, with Congress refusing to act, the president has pushed through in limited form by executive order: raising the minimum wage for federal contractors and trying to shrink the gender wage gap among federal contractors. He also mandated paid leave for federal workers. And this change has been painfully slow in coming. Obama ordered the Labor Department back in March 2014 to overhaul the overtime regulations. The overtime threshold has been changed just once since 1975, when it was set at $250 per week. Then in 2004, President George W. Bush bumped it to $455. The result? Inflation has steadily eaten away at the share of Americans who are guaranteed eligibility. Adjust for inflation and the collapse of the threshold is stark. Data from the St. Louis Federal Reserve (going back to 1979) show that in the late 1970s, the threshold was right at or slightly above the median worker's pay. Today it sits at around half!

title: Malia Obama joins protest against Trump over Dakota Access pipeline
text: Less than a week after her father left office with a nearly historically high approval rating, First Daughter Malia Obama has taken a limited step into politics. On Monday, four days after her father left the Oval Office, Malia showed her disappointment with the new commander-in-chief by joining a rally against his plans to revive the Dakota Access pipeline project. The 18-year-old student, who will attend Harvard University later this year, was one of approximately 100 people who gathered on Main Street at the Sundance Film Festival to express opposition to President Trump's plan to proceed with the controversial transport system. That decision followed months of protests. In his first week in office, Donald Trump reversed the decision, acting against the Standing Rock Sioux by signing an executive order that would allow the pipeline to proceed. That decision is the subject of Malia's protest.

title: Eleven things to let go of before the new year
text: The new year is approaching, and it is commonly a time when people begin to consider what they want to change in the coming year. The author states that they have not generally favoured the practice of making changes because of the new year, but suggests that the date can still be used as an occasion for change. The author recommends a brief period of reflection: considering whether one has followed one's dreams and passions over the past year, whether one was frequently caught up in the stresses of life, and whether judgement, negative self-talk and anger were a large part of one's days. According to the author, reflecting on how one has felt over the year and being honest about it provides an opportunity to understand how to adjust and move forward from that point, whether or not it is the new year. The author writes that, in their own life, when they do not pay attention to how they feel, what they create and what is happening in their life, and do not take responsibility for it, nothing changes: the situation stays the same, the same emotions or stagnant feelings recur, and there is no progress. When the author decides to take matters into their own hands, however, they see that they are not a victim of circumstances. The article then lists 11 things to let go of before the new year. The first is to stop negative self-talk, which is listed first because it is likely one of the most important. The more people speak poorly about themselves, to themselves or to others, the more they disempower themselves and strengthen the traits they wish to change. The recommendation is to observe it, note it and stop it, as it is not helpful. The second is to choose one bad eating habit and stop it.

title: Studies examine how media reporting on medicine affects science
text: A study of the dietary advice given by newspapers in the UK found “no credible scientific basis” for most claims. The “[m]isreporting of dietary advice” was found to be “widespread and may contribute to public misconceptions about food and health.” The effect may extend beyond the public. Scientists generally consider themselves uninfluenced by popular media, and a study set out to test this. Each week, The New York Times reports on scientific research, and the studies it reports on are subsequently cited more often than those it does not report on. This would suggest that the popular press has an impact. However, that is only one possible explanation. Outstanding articles may be both more likely to be covered by the media and independently more likely to be cited. The newspaper may simply have been identifying important science, without its publicity having any effect on future studies. Separating the two explanations required a specific event, which occurred in 1978. During a three-month strike, the newspaper continued to print copies but could not sell them to the public. This created a natural experiment. If the paper was only identifying important articles, the strike would have had no effect on the studies' impact. That was not the result. The studies highlighted during the strike months, when no one could read them, appeared to have no impact. A further question is whether the media simply amplify medical information to the medical community or also distort it. Systematic studies suggest that many stories about new medicines, for example, tend to overstate benefits, understate risks and costs, and fail to disclose relevant financial ties.

title: Trump's relationship with Florida attorney general could create scandal for Republicans
text: Many Republicans believe that if Donald Trump's presidential campaign is as unsuccessful as it appears it will be, they can contain the damage. Under this reasoning, if Trump fails, it is best to keep him at arm's length so that Republicans do not suffer too much as a result. That containment strategy now faces a test, as evidence emerges that Trump's controversial Trump University may have avoided criminal prosecution because of a relationship between Trump and Florida Attorney General Pam Bondi. Bondi denies that a $25,000 donation from Donald Trump is in any way connected to her office's decision not to pursue action against Trump University, despite dozens of complaints in Florida, her spokesman said. Bondi, who endorsed Trump in March, received the donation in 2013 through a political action committee raising money for her re-election. Bondi, who became prominent in conservative circles through repeated appearances on Fox News, reportedly received multiple complaints about Trump University's business practices, according to new documents released in the fraud litigation against Trump University. Bondi's office did not act as an advocate for the consumers defrauded by Trump University, as its role required, and decided against prosecuting the organization. The complaints show that several dissatisfied customers called the course a scam, and one man said it forced him into personal bankruptcy. Trump has recently announced a campaign event in Florida at which Bondi, who supports his nomination, will appear. Texas Governor Greg Abbott, who was the state's attorney general when legal action against Trump University was advancing, did not announce that the company faced a $5.4 million penalty for the way it had conducted business in the state. Trump University stopped doing business in the state shortly afterwards.

title: Turkey demands U.S. hand over ex-police investigator who testified in explosive New York trial
text: Turkey is turning up the heat. Its justice minister has told his U.S. counterpart that a former Turkish police investigator who testified this week at the New York trial of a Turkish banker is wanted by Ankara and must be swiftly sent back, ministry sources said on Friday. Huseyin Korkmaz took the stand at the trial of a Turkish banker charged with helping Iran dodge U.S. sanctions, a case that has badly strained ties between NATO allies Turkey and the United States. “It has been requested by our judicial offices that (Korkmaz) be temporarily arrested with the aim of being repatriated, based on alleged crimes,” Justice Minister Abdulhamit Gul wrote in a letter to U.S. Justice Secretary Jeff Sessions, according to the sources at his ministry. “We expect that the request is met on positive terms and the previously mentioned person be repatriated as soon as possible.” The Turkish government claims followers of U.S.-based cleric Fethullah Gulen, whom it blames for last year's failed military coup, are behind the U.S. case. Gulen has denied any role in the coup attempt. Gul did not hold back. “I want to point out that a fugitive, a terror suspect facing serious allegations, taking part in this case in your country as a witness is big enough a scandal,” he said, warning that the case could do irreparable damage to relations if action was not taken. A scandal? Korkmaz told the trial at Manhattan federal court this week that he feared he would be tortured if he returned to Turkey, where he led an investigation involving Turkish officials and Mehmet Hakan Atilla, the bank executive on trial in New York. Gul's letter also repeated Turkish allegations of contact between members of the judiciary who have handled the case and members of the Gulen network!

title: Doors slammed on reporters at secretive Kushner visa-for-cash pitch in China
text: What were they hiding? Organizers blocked journalists on Sunday from a publicly advertised event in Shanghai that dangled U.S. immigrant visas in front of Chinese investors willing to pour money into a real estate project linked to the family of President Donald Trump's son-in-law. The project is One Journal Square, a two-tower luxury apartment complex in New Jersey being developed by KABR Group and the Kushner Companies, which until recently was run by senior White House advisor Jared Kushner, husband of Trump's daughter Ivanka. The developers want to raise $150 million, or 15.4 percent of the project's funding, from investors through the EB-5 visa program, according to marketing materials posted by the event's organizer, immigration agency Qiaowai. The controversial EB-5 program lets wealthy foreigners effectively buy U.S. immigration visas for themselves and their families by investing at least $500,000 in certain development projects. And the press? Shut out. “Sorry, this is a private event,” said a man blocking journalists from entering a function room at the Four Seasons Hotel in Shanghai. Guests said Kushner's sister, Nicole Kushner Meyer, spoke for about 10 minutes, including about her family's humble roots. Humble roots, at a luxury hotel pitch! According to the New York Times, Meyer attended a similar event in Beijing on Saturday and told the audience of about 100 people the project “means a lot to me and my entire family”. Jared Kushner, whose White House portfolio includes relations with China, sold his stake in Kushner Companies to a family trust early this year.

title: Philadelphia slaps soda tax on sugary drinks as mayor beats Big Soda at its own game
text: Big Soda has finally lost one. Philadelphia Mayor Jim Kenney pulled off a victory that had slipped away from more than 40 U.S. public officials who took on the powerful U.S. soda industry, as the city council voted on Thursday to slap a tax on sweetened drinks. After a bitter, months-long war, the council voted 13-4 to approve a 1.5 cent-per-ounce tax on sugary and diet drinks starting in January. The council had already backed the plan in a preliminary vote last week, and no one expected the outcome to change. The City of Brotherly Love is now the biggest U.S. city with such a tax. Much smaller Berkeley, California, was the first. Similar efforts, including several led by former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg, were crushed by intense lobbying from groups like the American Beverage Association, which opposes the Philadelphia move and represents Coca-Cola Co and PepsiCo Inc. And the industry is not giving up: after Thursday's vote, the ABA vowed legal action to stop the tax. The vote was a major win for health advocates who say sugary drinks cause obesity and diabetes. But here is the twist. Experts noted those concerns were not Kenney's focus, or that of other backers, as they faced critics complaining that “nanny state” public health measures intrude on residents' personal lives. Instead, Kenney tore up the soda-tax advocate's playbook. He hammered home the cash injection the tax would bring to the city's depleted coffers. In the first year, the tax is projected to raise $91 million, and he pledged to spend the funds on public programs such as universal pre-kindergarten. Smart move? “If you want to tax something and people know where the money’s going to go, then it’s easier for them to get behind it,” Kenney said in an interview.

title: White House holds Christmas tree arrival ceremony
text: First Lady Melania Trump and Barron Trump received the official 2017 White House Christmas Tree today, in what supporters describe as a return of Christmas to the White House. The tree is a 19-and-a-half-foot Balsam fir from Wisconsin that was selected in September. title: Ford CEO says company will proceed with $2.5 billion plant in Mexico
text: The focus should arguably be on the EPA and other government agencies, which create a very difficult environment for manufacturing goods in America. We don't get anything. Does Mexico come here and build factories here? We lose a fortune with every deal that adds jobs overseas,” Trump said. Fields defended Ford's record on supporting American jobs. “We've created 25,000 jobs [in the U.S.] since 2011, and going forward over the next four years we've agreed to either retain or add another 8,500 jobs,” Fields said. “The amount of money that we invest in [research and development] here is more than companies like Apple.” Ford invested nearly $7 billion in research and development in the U.S. in 2014 alone, Fields said. The Republican presidential frontrunner's criticism of Ford focused largely on Ford's plans to invest $2.5 billion in its Mexican operations. In October, Trump took credit for Ford supposedly canceling those plans and opening a new factory in Ohio instead. However, Ford said it planned to proceed with its $2.5 billion expansion in Mexico. Its decision to move production of a line of trucks from Mexico to Ohio was made four years ago during union negotiations.

title: Paul Ryan's comments on Iowa insurance market support case for Medicare for all, writer argues
text: When people are allowed to speak, they sometimes end up stating the position their opponents have held all along, even if unintentionally. In this case, liberals should accept the argument for Medicare for all that Speaker Paul Ryan (R-WI) has provided, and should continue to remind him of it. While attempting to portray the Affordable Care Act negatively, Ryan inadvertently made a strong argument for Medicare for all. On April 8, 2017, Ryan wrote on Twitter: “With another insurer leaving the Iowa insurance market, more Americans will be left without a choice when it comes to their health care.” He followed it with a second post: “Five Iowa counties will now be left with just two health insurers, while the rest will only have one option. This is unacceptable.” First, if Iowa had implemented Obamacare properly, it would have its own health exchange rather than directing residents to the national website. That would also have given Iowa insurers the ability to work directly with the state. Second, when for-profit companies are given the ability to interfere with people's care for the sake of profit, and to try to demonstrate that a program is not working, they will do so. Therefore, Ryan's statements amount to a strong argument for Medicare for all, or at least for a public option.
